report:
**Conclusion: probably yes, but the evidence is limited enough that monk’s pepper (Vitex agnus-castus; chasteberry) should be viewed as an optional, not proven first-line, PMS treatment.**

The strongest individual evidence is a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial of 170 women over three cycles. It found that a specific monk’s-pepper fruit extract improved a combined PMS symptom score and produced more responders than placebo. This supports a real benefit, particularly for typical physical and mood symptoms, but it tests one standardized extract—not all supplements sold as monk’s pepper.  
https://www.bmj.com/content/322/7279/134

Systematic-review evidence is directionally favorable, but trials have used differing preparations, doses, outcome measures, and study designs. That heterogeneity makes the size of benefit and best product/dose uncertain.  
https://www.repositorio.unifesp.br/items/1a79b680-d15d-4e08-b9be-447991c7f479

Importantly, the 2023 ACOG guideline notes small studies suggesting symptom improvement and tolerability, but does **not** recommend chasteberry because further research is needed. Thus, this is evidence against treating the answer as an unequivocal “yes,” especially for severe PMS or PMDD.  
https://www.aafp.org/afp/2024/1200/practice-guidelines-premenstrual-disorders.pdf

Safety data are relatively reassuring for short-term use, but “natural” does not mean risk-free. Discuss it with a clinician before use if pregnant or breastfeeding, taking regular medicines, or if symptoms are severe, new, or interfere with daily life. Use a symptom diary across at least two cycles to confirm PMS and objectively assess whether any treatment helps.  
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/chasteberry
